parsed.study_design: Cross-sectional field survey with aggregated consumption-record analysis and a randomized scenario study
parsed.population_and_sample: Study 1: 76 adult household managers in metered and unmetered Hampshire communities; Study 2: 64 adults recruited in Southampton
parsed.exposure: Household water metering and consumption-based charging versus unmetered flat-rate charging, examined in interaction with perceived or experimentally assigned water-shortage severity
parsed.outcome: Self-reported water-conservation behavior, conservation intentions, concern about overconsumption, and area-level changes in water consumption
parsed.rationale: The paper empirically evaluates whether household metering promotes reduced domestic water consumption during shortages (Study 1, pp. 738–743; Study 2, pp. 743–746). Although metering and tariff structure are relevant administrative or governance factors, the measured outcome is consumer conservation behavior and aggregate resource use—not household access, connection, service availability, reliability, quantity received, affordability, or exclusion. It therefore has the wrong outcome for this review.
